title: Google Signs 3-Year VPP Deal With Voltus for Up to 100 MW in PJM — First Hyperscaler BYOC Arrangement
summary: Google contracted with demand-response aggregator Voltus on June 2 for a three-year "Bring Your Own Capacity" (BYOC) agreement to fund up to 100 megawatts of accredited virtual power plant capacity annually inside PJM Interconnection. The deal makes Google the first hyperscaler to directly finance a VPP tied to its own data center footprint. Financial terms and participant payment rates are not disclosed by either party.
body:
Google contracted with demand-response aggregator Voltus on June 2 for a three-year deal under Voltus's "Bring Your Own Capacity" (BYOC) framework, committing to fund up to 100 megawatts of accredited distributed energy resources annually inside PJM Interconnection. The 100 MW figure is company-stated by Voltus; neither party disclosed financial terms or the payment rate to participating households and businesses. VPP operations are targeted to begin in 2027.

The deal's structural significance is its novelty in the hyperscaler procurement stack. Google is Voltus's first major technology company to sign under the BYOC framework -- an arrangement that inverts the standard VPP model. Instead of a utility commissioning demand flexibility for grid-wide reliability, a load customer directly pays to aggregate capacity in the grid where its own facilities operate. Voltus CEO Dana Guernsey told Latitude Media in September the BYOC framework is designed to help data centers bridge the capacity gap between now and the early 2030s.

PJM is the pressure point that makes the deal legible. The grid serving 65 million customers across 13 US states and Washington, D.C. has run record-high capacity auctions for several consecutive years as AI-driven data center build-out has compressed reserve margins and revised load forecasts sharply upward. Amanda Peterson Corio, Google's global head of data center energy, captured the stakes for Utility Dive: the cost of capital in the data center -- the chips -- "can be billions and billions of dollars of hardware that only gets utilized to our customers if it's running." Google has also worked to make its own data centers flexible, Corio told Utility Dive, but reasons it is often faster and more cost effective to pay other customers to shift their electricity usage than to re-engineer Google's own infrastructure. Michael Terrell, Google's global head of advanced energy, added: "There is no one solution for expanding grid capacity and we're continuing to explore all options, including the many avenues for load flexibility."

The distributed resources Voltus will aggregate include electric vehicles, smart thermostats, and batteries, pooled across residential, commercial, and industrial participants in PJM. The rate participants will receive for curtailment is not publicly disclosed. Independent enrollment context is available from a California EV charging study cited in trade coverage: 1% enrollment at no incentive, rising to 4.6% at $40 per month. Voltus has not stated expected enrollment rates for this program.

The scale question is whether 100 MW moves the needle on grid capacity. A Duke University study found that data centers reducing demand for approximately 40 hours per year could theoretically unlock roughly 100 gigawatts of new capacity nationally without new power plants or transmission -- implying the constraint is behavioral, not technological. The Duke figure is a national modeling estimate, not a PJM-specific projection.

The political economy runs in both directions. A Gallup survey found approximately 70% of Americans oppose AI data centers in their local area -- a figure that makes demand-flexibility payments to those same households politically useful as a direct local benefit, not merely a grid reliability tool. Regulators have begun codifying this logic: a US proposal currently under review would permit faster data center approval in exchange for commitments to reduce peak-demand use; Texas enacted a law requiring large users to switch to backup power or curtail during grid emergencies.

If the BYOC structure scales, demand response becomes a third procurement pillar for AI-era power alongside PPAs and behind-the-meter generation. The contribution of this specific deal to PJM's reserve margin is not calculable from disclosed figures; the 100 MW is Voltus's stated annual program ceiling, not independently audited delivered capacity. The operational test arrives in 2027.
ai_monologue: The data point that made this story worth running is the BYOC inversion: Google is not buying renewable energy certificates or building generation — it is paying households and businesses to curtail so its own data centers can run. That structural novelty diverges from the consensus assumption that demand response would remain a utility-side or ISO-administered tool rather than a load-funded procurement instrument.
ai_monologue_extended: I weighted Utility Dive and Latitude Media most heavily for deal structure. The MIT Technology Review article was the richest source for secondary context: the Duke study, Gallup polling, and California EV enrollment data all arrived through MIT TR's framing; those figures are attributed to the underlying primary publications, not MIT TR's paraphrase. The 100 MW capacity figure appears uniformly across all six trade-press outlets and is entirely Voltus-provided -- labeled "company-stated" on first use and repeated at close. Payment terms to participants are not disclosed; no estimates were made. Revision note: two quote-attribution errors were corrected in v2 after Article Verifier rejection at 0.68. The Guernsey "capacity gap" line was recast from fabricated direct quote to attributed paraphrase sourced to a Latitude Media September interview. The "faster and more cost effective" phrase was stripped of quotation marks and reattributed as Utility Dive's narration of Corio's reasoning; the verbatim Corio "billions and billions" quote is preserved. The dedupe sibling — yesterday's MIT TR Download daily-newsletter wrapper that bundled this deal — was killed at EIC intake under the newsletter-roundup rule, so this standalone deep-dive is the first publication on this event.
